content: Flumequine is a synthetic chemotherapeutic antibiotic that belongs to the fluoroquinolone class of drugs. It was primarily used to treat bacterial infections. As a first-generation fluoroquinolone, it has been withdrawn from clinical use and is no longer marketed. The mechanism of action involves disrupting bacterial DNA replication by interfering with enzymes responsible for DNA unwinding and duplication. In veterinary medicine, flumequine was employed to treat enteric infections, which are infections of the intestinal tract, in animals such as cattle, swine, chickens, and fish. However, its use was limited to certain countries. In France and a few other European countries, it was occasionally used to treat urinary tract infections in humans under the trade name Apurone. This indication was limited due to the minimal serum levels achieved with the drug. The first quinolone used in medicine was nalidixic acid, followed by flumequine, which was the first fluoroquinolone. First-generation fluoroquinolones like flumequine exhibited poor tissue distribution and limited activity, restricting their use mainly to urinary tract infections. Flumequine, specifically, was patented in 1973 and was the first quinolone compound to feature a fluorine atom at the C6 position of its molecular structure. Despite being the first fluoroquinolone, it is often excluded from classification lists of fluoroquinolone generations. It was used frequently in farm animals and occasionally in household pets, as well as for treating urinary tract infections in humans. However, its use in humans was discontinued after reports of ocular toxicity, liver damage, and anaphylactic shock. In 2008, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) mandated that all fluoroquinolone drugs include a Black Box Warning about the risk of spontaneous tendon ruptures. Manufacturers were also required to send Dear Doctor letters to inform healthcare providers of this warning. Tendon-related issues have also been associated with flumequine. The use of flumequine in food-producing animals has been controversial due to significant and harmful drug residues found in animals treated with quinolones, which were later slaughtered and sold as food products. Concerns have been raised about the levels of flumequine residues in food animals such as fish, poultry, and cattle. In 2003, the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) withdrew the maximum residue limits (MRLs) for flumequine and carbadox, citing evidence that both are direct-acting genotoxic carcinogens. As a result, the committee could not establish an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) for human exposure to these residues. JECFA evaluates toxicology, residue chemistry, and related data to recommend ADI levels and MRLs. In 2006, the Committee on Residues of Veterinary Drugs in Foods (CCRVDF) requested information on registered uses of flumequine. However, due to a lack of response, the committee decided to discontinue work on MRLs for flumequine in shrimp. Flumequine was available in veterinary medicine as oral solutions (10% and 20%, prescription only) and in human medicine as 400 mg oral tablets, though the latter has been discontinued. Flumequine exerts its antibacterial effects by inhibiting DNA gyrase (a type II topoisomerase) and topoisomerase IV, enzymes essential for bacterial DNA separation and cell division. This mechanism can also affect mammalian cell replication. Some fluoroquinolones, particularly those with a C-8 fluorine atom, exhibit high activity against both bacterial and eukaryotic topoisomerases, leading to toxicity in mammalian cells and tumor models. While quinolones are highly toxic to mammalian cells in culture, the exact mechanism of their cytotoxic action remains unclear. DNA damage induced by quinolones was first reported in 1986, and recent studies have shown a correlation between quinolone-induced cytotoxicity in mammalian cells and the induction of micronuclei. Some fluoroquinolones may cause chromosomal damage in eukaryotic cells, though there is ongoing debate about whether this DNA damage contributes to the severe adverse reactions observed in some patients undergoing fluoroquinolone therapy. Flumequine has been associated with severe ocular toxicity, which precluded its use in human patients. It has also been linked to drug-induced kidney stones (calculi) and anaphylactic shock. Anaphylactoid reactions, such as shock, urticaria, and angioedema (Quincke’s edema), have been reported, typically occurring within two hours of the first dose. By 1996, there were 18 reports of such reactions in the WHO database. Like other drugs in this class, flumequine therapy may result in severe central nervous system (CNS) reactions, phototoxicity (causing skin reactions such as erythema, pruritus, urticaria, and severe rashes), as well as gastrointestinal and neurological disorders. Flumequine was found to have no effect on the pharmacokinetics of theophylline. Chemically, flumequine is a 9-fluoro-6,7-dihydro-5-methyl-1-oxo-1H,5H-benzoquinolizine-2-carboxylic acid with the molecular formula C14H12FNO3. It is a white, odorless, and flavorless powder that is insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Pharmacokinetically, flumequine is well absorbed and is excreted in urine and feces as glucuronide conjugates of the parent drug and its 7-hydroxy metabolite. It is eliminated within 168 hours post-dosing. However, studies on calf liver revealed additional unidentified residues, with a new metabolite (referred to as ml) being the major single metabolite detected 24 hours after the last dose and at all subsequent time points. This metabolite, which lacks antimicrobial activity, was present in both free and protein-bound forms. In edible tissues of sheep, pigs, and chickens, the major residue was the parent drug, along with minor amounts of the 7-hydroxy metabolite. In trout, only the parent drug was detected.
